prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: After, Elinor, Lipper

outputs.L1:
After Elinor Lipper

The creature that had once been a man  
handed over his petition—  
a stained and grimy scrap—  
to his lord and master:  
a petition asking to be transferred  
to the status of a horse.

“You son-of-a-whore,” the master bellowed,  
kicking him for good measure.  
“What do you mean by this?”

The creature that had once been a man,  
having considered his petition deeply,  
answered:

“If I were a horse, I would have  
one day off in ten. As I am,  
I have none. As a horse,  
I could rest now and again  
during work. As a former man,  
I cannot. As a horse,  
I would be expected to perform work  
equal to my strength.  
As a prisoner, I am always hungry;  
and hungry, I work less and get less bread,  
so that I can barely stand.

“A horse gets a stable  
and two blankets. I have  
no blankets, no jacket.  
If a driver beats a horse too hard,  
he is punished, for a horse is precious.  
If the brigadiers beat and kick me,  
it is like beating a tree.  
So you see, a prisoner is nothing here.  
But a horse? A horse is something.”

Inside the frozen  
and broken vista, the plea carried  
a ring of truth, heard even  
by the lord and master,  
who had previously been a man himself,  
and who, when no other former men could see,  
attached that name to the page,  
granting the horse  
a stable and two blankets.
outputs.L2:
After Elinor Lipper

The being who had once been human  
presented his request—  
a dirty, blotched piece of paper—  
to the man who ruled over him,  
his lord and owner.  
In it, he asked to be reclassified  
as a horse.

“You bastard,” roared the master,  
adding a kick for emphasis.  
“What is this supposed to mean?”

The creature who had once been a man,  
after long and serious thought,  
gave his answer:

“If I were a horse,  
I would be allowed one free day in ten.  
Now, I receive none.

If I were a horse,  
I could pause from time to time  
while working.  
As a man who has been stripped of being a man,  
I cannot.

If I were a horse,  
no one would demand more labor from me  
than my body could bear.  
But as a prisoner,  
I am kept constantly hungry;  
because I am hungry, I work poorly,  
and because I work poorly, I am given less bread,  
until I can scarcely remain on my feet.

A horse is given a stall  
and two blankets.  
I have no blankets  
and no coat.

If a driver thrashes a horse too brutally,  
he is punished,  
because a horse has value.  
But when the brigadiers strike me,  
when they kick me,  
it is no different to them  
from beating a tree.

So you understand:  
a prisoner counts for nothing here.  
But a horse—  
a horse matters.”

In that frozen, shattered landscape,  
the request sounded true,  
even to the lord and master,  
who himself had once been a man.  
And when none of the other former men  
were there to witness it,  
he signed his name to the paper,  
and granted the horse  
a stable and two blankets.
outputs.L3:
A prisoner once submitted a petition to his master, asking for an unusual change in his status: he wished to be reclassified as a horse. Though the request seemed strange at first, the prisoner explained that it was not made in jest, but out of desperation and careful observation.

He argued that horses were treated with far greater consideration than prisoners. A horse was given rest when it was tired, shelter when the weather was harsh, and blankets to protect it from the cold. Its food and workload were measured according to its strength, because a weakened horse could not serve its master well. In contrast, prisoners were driven beyond endurance, regardless of hunger, exhaustion, or illness.

The prisoner described his own condition plainly. He was always hungry, forced to labor beyond his strength, and denied even the most basic protection from cold, heat, and fatigue. While animals were preserved because they were useful property, prisoners were treated as though their suffering did not matter.

He also pointed out a bitter injustice: anyone who harmed a horse was punished, because a horse had recognized value. But a prisoner could be beaten, starved, or worked to collapse with little concern, as if his life were worth less than that of an animal.

The master, upon reading the petition, recognized the painful truth in the prisoner’s words. Moved by the argument, he granted the request. The prisoner was given the status of a horse, along with a place in the stable and two blankets for warmth. Thus, by asking to be treated as an animal, he finally received a measure of care that had been denied to him as a man.
outputs.L4:
The prisoner stood before his master with his cap crushed between his hands and his eyes fixed on the ground. He had been summoned after making a request so strange that even the guards had laughed at it before sending him on. Now, in the bare office where orders were signed and punishments decided, he repeated it plainly.

“Master,” he said, “I ask to be reclassified as a horse.”

The master looked up from his desk. He was a hard man, feared throughout the camp for his temper and cruelty. Men were beaten for moving too slowly, starved for disobedience, and worked until they collapsed. He had heard petitions before: requests for lighter labor, for medicine, for permission to bury the dead, for a crust of bread. Most were refused before the speaker finished. But this request amused him.

“A horse?” he said. “You are a man.”

The prisoner raised his head only slightly. “That is why I am asking.”

The master leaned back. “Explain yourself.”

The prisoner swallowed. His body showed the camp’s arithmetic clearly: ribs under skin, cracked hands, a face hollowed by hunger and sleeplessness. Yet his voice was steady.

“A man here is sent to the quarry before dawn,” he said. “He pulls, carries, digs, and lifts until darkness. If he falls, he is beaten. If he cannot rise, he is dragged aside. If he dies, another man is brought to take his place.”

He paused, then continued.

“A horse also works. But a horse is not worked past the point of uselessness. When a horse stumbles, the driver checks its legs. When it is ill, someone calls for the farrier. When it is wounded, the wound is cleaned. A horse is too valuable to lose carelessly.”

The master’s amusement began to fade.

The prisoner went on. “A man sleeps where he can, on boards or mud, crowded among the sick and dying. Rain comes through the roof. Cold comes through the walls. Lice and fever spread from body to body. If he coughs blood, he is told to stand up for roll call.”

He looked toward the window, beyond which the stables stood. They were better built than the barracks.

“A horse has straw,” he said. “A horse has a stall. A horse is sheltered from the rain, because dampness weakens the lungs. A horse is covered in winter, because cold stiffens the limbs. A horse is given space enough to lie down.”

The master’s jaw tightened, but he did not interrupt.

“A man eats what is thrown to him,” the prisoner said. “Thin soup, black bread, sometimes nothing. He works hungry, sleeps hungry, wakes hungry. His strength is demanded, but never restored.”

He glanced at the master’s polished boots.

“A horse is fed oats. A horse is watered. Its ration is measured not by contempt, but by need. If the horse is expected to pull, it must be given the strength to pull. If it grows thin, someone notices. If it refuses food, someone worries.”

The room had become very quiet. Outside, a cart rattled past. The sound of hooves struck the hard ground with a rhythm both ordinary and accusatory.

The prisoner pressed on, knowing that if he stopped now he might never again be allowed to speak.

“A man may be struck for any reason,” he said. “For looking up. For looking down. For walking too slowly. For being too weak to walk faster. His bones may be broken, and it is called discipline. His blood may be spilled, and it is called order.”

He drew a breath.

“A horse may be whipped, yes. But not blindly. Not until its back is ruined. Not until it cannot work. A man may be destroyed in anger, but a horse is protected from anger because it has worth.”

At that, the master rose from his chair. The prisoner lowered his eyes again, expecting a blow. But none came.

The master walked to the window and looked out at the stables. They were clean, orderly, maintained. Each animal had a number, a record, an assigned ration. Their shoes were checked; their coats were brushed; their illnesses were logged. They were property, and because they were property, they were preserved.

The men in the barracks were also numbered, also recorded, also assigned. Yet they were not preserved. They were consumed.

The master turned back. “And if I grant this request,” he said slowly, “you accept the duties of a horse?”

“Yes, Master.”

“You will pull carts?”

“I pull them now.”

“You will haul stones?”

“I haul them now.”

“You will obey the driver?”

“I obey now.”

“You will be tied, housed, inspected, and used for labor?”

“I am tied, housed, inspected, and used for labor now.”

The master stared at him. The answer had no rebellion in it, no sarcasm that could be punished openly. It was simply exact. That was what made it intolerable.

The prisoner added, “The only difference is that, as a horse, I would be fed enough to work. I would be allowed to rest enough to stand. I would be sheltered enough not to freeze. I would receive treatment if injured. I would not be killed wastefully.”

The master sat down again. He took up his pen, then set it down. He wanted to reject the request, but he could not find the flaw in it. The camp had been built on the claim that some people were less than human. Yet the prisoner had carried that claim to its logical end and discovered something worse: even an animal stood higher in the order of care.

To call the prisoner a man imposed no obligation here. To call him a horse did.

At last the master pulled a form toward him and wrote the order. The prisoner was to be transferred to the labor stables and entered among the draft animals. He would be assigned a stall, rationed according to labor output, examined for injury, and protected from unnecessary damage.

When the guard read the order aloud, the men outside laughed again, but uneasily this time. The prisoner did not laugh. He bowed, took back his cap, and left the office.

That evening, for the first time in months, he slept on straw. He was still imprisoned. He was still owned, still watched, still forced to labor. Nothing about his bondage had ended. Yet he was warmer than he had been in the barracks. In the morning he was given food measured for endurance rather than starvation. When a sore on his shoulder opened under the harness, a stable hand cleaned it.

The improvement was not mercy. It was not justice. It was not recognition of his humanity. It was the opposite: he had survived by persuading his oppressor to deny it completely.

And that was the horror revealed by his petition. In that world, a man could be starved, beaten, exposed, and spent without concern. But a horse had value. A horse represented labor to be maintained, property to be protected, strength to be preserved.

The prisoner had not risen in dignity. He had descended in name and, by doing so, risen in treatment.

The master granted the request because its logic could not be denied. The camp had already made men into beasts. The prisoner merely asked to receive the care given to one.
outputs.L5:
After the ceremony ended, Elinor stood quietly at the edge of the garden, watching the evening light settle over the trees. She had always believed that change arrived loudly, with grand announcements and unmistakable signs, but this time it came gently. A letter from Lipper lay folded in her hand, its words simple yet powerful enough to alter everything she had planned.

Lipper had written about forgiveness, about the strange paths people take before they understand what truly matters. Elinor read the letter twice, then looked toward the road leading out of town. After years of waiting for others to decide her future, she finally felt ready to choose it for herself.

With a calm breath, Elinor placed the letter in her pocket and began to walk. Whatever came next, she knew it would be hers.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem inspired by Elinor Lipper’s accounts of Soviet labor camps, about a prisoner petitioning to be treated as a horse because animals receive better care than men.
counterfactuals.output:
**Petition**

To the Commandant,  
to the clerk with the thaw-cracked hands,  
to the stamp pad black as frozen blood,

I submit this request:

Strike out my name.  
Enter me under livestock.

I have considered the advantages.  
A horse receives oats in a sack,  
not slogans in the mouth.  
A horse is brushed  
where a man is searched.  
A horse has a blanket  
because a back is valuable  
if it belongs to hauling.

I can haul.

Harness me to the sledge.  
Count my ribs with concern.  
Say: this one is weakening,  
give him mash,  
check his hooves,  
do not waste good animals.

I have watched them steam in the dawn,  
the horses,  
their breath making brief churches in the air.  
A stable has straw.  
A stable has walls that mean shelter,  
not punishment.  
When a horse stumbles,  
someone curses the road.

When a man falls,  
someone curses the man.

Comrade Commandant,  
I do not ask for freedom.  
That would be absurd,  
like asking winter to remember leaves.

I ask only for a sensible category:  
bay, gelding, draft;  
fit for timber;  
needs rest;  
ration increased.

Remove from my file  
the dangerous particulars—  
father’s name, charge, sentence,  
the place where a soul is supposed to be.  
Replace them with measurements:  
height at withers,  
condition of teeth,  
capacity for work.

I will answer to a whistle.  
I will not speak of justice.  
I will lower my head  
and take the bit of iron  
as if it were bread.

Only let the doctor come  
before the knacker.  
Let someone notice  
the sores under the collar.  
Let someone say,  
not out of pity,  
but accounting:

This animal must be kept alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a bleak narrative poem titled “After Elinor Lipper” in which a camp inmate asks his overseer to transfer him from the status of prisoner to the status of horse, explaining why a horse has more rights.
counterfactuals.output:
# After Elinor Lipper

At dawn, when the horn tore sleep from the barracks  
and the cold had already counted our ribs,  
I stepped from the line and lifted my cap  
to the man with the crop and the ledger.

“Sir,” I said, “there is an error in your book.  
You have written me down as prisoner.  
Cross it out. Make me horse.”

He laughed, not loudly—  
a dry hinge in the frozen yard.  
Behind him the stable steamed in the dark,  
warm as a rumor of God.

“Horse?” he said.

“Yes, sir. Horse.”

For a horse, I told him, has a name  
even if it is only Gray or Mare.  
A horse has straw beneath him  
and iron on his feet to keep the stones away.  
A horse is not struck for limping  
until the limp is examined.  
His sores are washed.  
His teeth are counted with concern.  
If he coughs, someone listens.

A horse is given oats,  
not because he deserves them  
but because he must pull tomorrow.  
A horse may lower his head to water  
and no one calls it theft.  
A horse’s flank is brushed  
where ours are searched.  
His mane is combed  
where our hair is shorn and swept.

If a horse falls,  
men gather with ropes.  
If he cannot rise,  
they curse the mud, the load, the weather—  
anything but the horse.  
And if at last they shoot him,  
they do it quickly,  
as though there were still a law  
somewhere inside the hand.

“Sir,” I said, “I too can pull.  
Harness me to the cart of stones.  
Let me sleep standing if I must.  
Brand me with your number,  
but call it ownership, not sentence.  
Give me a stall, a bucket,  
one armful of hay’s mercy.  
Let the veterinarian look into my mouth  
and say: this one may last the winter.”

The overseer tapped his boot with the crop.  
Snow fell, careful and indifferent,  
covering the ditch, the fence, the dead,  
as if the world had learned from paper  
how to erase a name.

Behind me the line breathed in rags.  
Before me the stable breathed in warmth.  
A horse stamped once, impatient, alive.  
The overseer smiled.

“You are mistaken,” he said.  
“A horse is property.”

I bowed my head.  
“Exactly, sir.  
Then someone would lose by my dying.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a prose-poem in a stark, historical style about dehumanization in a gulag: a starving prisoner argues that horses are valued more than people, and the commandant reluctantly grants the request.
counterfactuals.output:
In the ledger there were columns for men and columns for horses.

The men were counted at dawn, when the frost still had teeth. They stood in striped rags with their names reduced to numbers, their faces reduced to steam. If one fell, another shoulder closed the gap. The column must be complete.

The horses were counted at the stable, under a roof patched twice before winter. Their ribs were noted with concern. Their hooves were inspected. Their ration was written in a careful hand: oats, hay, salt. A horse, the quartermaster said, was property of the state. A horse could haul timber. A horse must be preserved.

One prisoner, hollow as a spoon, came before the commandant.

“Comrade Commandant,” he said, “I request to be transferred to the horse list.”

The clerk laughed once, then stopped.

The commandant looked up from the stove’s red eye. “What is this?”

“A horse receives feed,” the prisoner said. “A horse receives shelter. If a horse is lame, work is adjusted. If a horse dies, there is an investigation.”

The room held its breath. Outside, the camp scraped at the earth with dull axes.

“I can pull,” the prisoner continued. “I can carry. I can freeze standing. I have forgotten how to speak except when ordered. I ask only that I be treated according to my value.”

The commandant’s face tightened, not from pity but from recognition, as if a nail had found the old hole. He knew the regulations. He knew the arithmetic of survival. Men arrived in trains. Horses did not.

At last he signed a scrap of paper.

“Give him the horse ration,” he said quietly. “For three days.”

The clerk wrote it down without meeting anyone’s eyes.

That evening the prisoner received a double ladle and a place near the stable wall, where the animals breathed warm clouds into the dark. He ate slowly, like a man committing theft from his own grave.

In the morning, the guards called numbers.

From the stable came no answer, only the stamping of hooves, and the soft, living sound of creatures the state had decided not to waste.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary piece, grim and ironic, where a man in a prison camp submits a petition to become a horse, listing the practical benefits—rest, food, blankets, protection from beatings.
counterfactuals.output:
To the Commandant, by way of the clerk who still has ink:

I respectfully petition to be transferred from the human category to the equine.

My reasons are practical. A horse is not woken before dawn to account for the missing dead. A horse is allowed to stand when tired, and when it can no longer stand, this is understood as a condition rather than an offense. A horse receives oats, or at least hay; water is brought to it in a bucket not previously used for lime. In winter a horse may be issued a blanket, and if the blanket is thin, no one explains that the Fatherland is cold too.

Furthermore, a horse is beaten only to make it move. This is a great refinement. Among men, blows are distributed for slowness, haste, coughing, silence, looking up, looking down, and once, in my case, for having a face reminiscent of an uncle of the guard. I do not object to discipline, but I ask that it be made purposeful.

A horse is valuable because it can pull a cart. I can pull a cart. A horse is counted because it represents property. I am already counted. A horse may not speak. This I can learn quickly; indeed I have made progress.

If approved, I request a stall near the wall, away from the draught, and permission to forget my name. In exchange I offer my back, my teeth if they remain useful, and my gratitude, which is small but durable.

The clerk read the petition twice. Then he laughed, which proved the man had written something comic. He stamped it DENIED, which proved the man was still a man.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a haunting free verse adaptation of an anecdote from Elinor Lipper, emphasizing “former men,” brutal masters, hunger, cold, and the absurd truth that in the camp a horse is worth more than a prisoner.
counterfactuals.output:
In the ledger of winter  
we were not names,  
not even numbers with warmth inside them,  
but former men—  
the phrase hung on us  
like a torn coat stiff with frost.

Former teachers, former clerks,  
former fathers with hands that remembered bread,  
former believers in a door opening,  
in a spoon lowered toward a bowl  
because a human mouth was waiting.

The masters had boots,  
voices,  
the clean violence of men  
who slept beneath roofs.  
They could make hunger stand at attention.  
They could order the cold  
to enter our bones  
and it obeyed.

We learned to move as shadows move:  
thinly, without complaint,  
careful not to spend breath  
on anything so useless  
as hope.

Then came the horse.

Steam rose from its nostrils  
like a little factory of life.  
Its flanks were brushed,  
its feed measured,  
its rest protected by rules  
more sacred than any prayer  
we had smuggled into the camp.

Do not overwork the horse,  
they said.

And we, who dragged logs  
through snow up to the knees,  
who fell and were kicked awake,  
who chewed at sleep as if it were crust,  
understood the law at last:

a horse had value.

A horse could pull.  
A horse could be counted on a requisition form,  
replaced only with difficulty,  
entered in ink  
as property worth preserving.

But a prisoner—  
a former man—  
was plentiful as snow,  
and snow was shoveled aside.

So we watched the animal eat  
while our bellies clenched like fists.  
We watched them throw a blanket  
over its dark, trembling back,  
while the wind opened our rags  
and read our ribs.

No one laughed.  
The joke was too perfect,  
too immense,  
the kind only a kingdom of barbed wire  
could tell:

that mercy had hooves,  
that pity was kept in a stable,  
that in the frozen arithmetic of the camp  
one horse  
outweighed a hundred men  
who had once been men,  
and were still, terribly,  
hungry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
